99.title: The Jesus Prayer
99.hook: Orthodox Christians repeat Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, with the breath
99.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me', often many times a day, sometimes with a prayer rope and in rhythm with the breath. Many Catholic, Anglican and Protestant Christians use it too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ACTS: adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication. Your line was a shape helps.

Paul tells one of his churches, in the King James Bible: "Pray without ceasing." Taken literally, they're a problem: you have a job, dishes, sleep. How could anyone pray all the time? An old Russian book, written down in the 1800s by an unknown author, The Way of a Pilgrim, tells of a wanderer who hears those words read in church and can't let them go. He walks from town to town, asking priests and monks how it's done. Most give him sermons. Finally an old monk gives him something much smaller: one sentence, said over and over, until it begins to say itself.
screen: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.` → `A WANDERER ASKS HOW.` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: The sentence is the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Many add: a sinner. It's a short prayer with very old roots. On the road out of Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus hears Jesus passing and shouts, in the King James: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." People tell him to be quiet; he shouts louder. And in Jesus's story of two men praying in the temple, the tax collector can't even look up; he just says, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Put those two cries together: the Jesus Prayer. By the fourth and fifth centuries, monks in the Egyptian desert repeated short prayers like this all day while they worked. Over centuries the practice was treasured especially in the Orthodox churches, in the monasteries of Mount Athos in Greece, and in Russia. It's sometimes called hesychasm, from the Greek for stillness. Many use a prayer rope, a loop of woven knots, one knot for each prayer. Many join it to the breath: breathing in, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God; breathing out, have mercy on me. And mercy here isn't just let me off. In Greek, have mercy on me is eleison me, the same verb sung in the old church cry, Kyrie eleison, Lord have mercy. Its root, eleos, carries compassion, kindness poured out. Western Christians, Catholic, Anglican and Protestant, have taken up the prayer too. The pilgrim says that in time, it started praying in him, even as he walked.

segments.voice: If you pray, say it ten times, slowly, with your breath, in on Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, out on have mercy on me, counting on your fingers if it helps. Don't rush; when your mind wanders, just come back to the words. If you don't pray, breathe and listen to the words as someone else's prayer, or rest on a single word, like mercy.
Hesychasm: stillness, sought by repeating a short prayer like the Jesus Prayer, a blind man's shout and a tax collector's whisper, said with the breath.
Your line: have mercy on me. Tomorrow, day one hundred, and a shepherd's psalm. See you there.

100.title: Praying the Psalms (Psalm 23)
100.hook: for three thousand years people have prayed with borrowed words
100.howItsDone: Christians pray and sing the Psalms in worship every week, and monks and many others pray them daily; the Rule of Saint Benedict covers all 150 in a week, and the Book of Common Prayer in a month. Psalm 23 is read at many Christian funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hesychasm: the Jesus Prayer, said with the breath. Your line was have mercy on me. Today: one hundred days.

Think of the times you had no words of your own. At a funeral. In the night after bad news. On a day so good you wanted to shout. People often reach for borrowed words: a song, a poem, someone else's line that says it better. At funerals in many countries, even people who never go to church find they know one set of words by heart. The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. Those words come from a book of a hundred and fifty prayers and songs, prayed in one form or another for close to three thousand years: the prayer book inside the Bible.
screen: `WHEN YOU HAVE NO WORDS.` → `BORROWED WORDS.` → `THE PRAYER BOOK INSIDE THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Psalter is the book of Psalms, used for praying. It comes from the Greek for a stringed instrument, because these were songs. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises. Tradition links many to King David, the shepherd boy who became king around three thousand years ago, though many were written by others, over centuries. Surprise: they're not all praise. There's joy, but also rage, fear, loneliness, and complaints that sound almost rude, words for every mood. Jesus prayed them: his cry on the cross, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, is the first line of Psalm twenty-two. Jews have prayed the psalms every day for many centuries, and still do. Monks under the Rule of Saint Benedict pray all hundred and fifty weekly; the Anglican prayer book walks through them every month. Now the most famous one, in the King James Bible: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters." Where it prints LORD in capitals, the Hebrew has God's own personal name, which Jews, out of reverence, do not say aloud. It doesn't pretend life is easy: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me." Notice the turn. The first lines talk about God; in the dark valley, it talks to him: thou art with me. That's what borrowed words can do. You start by reading. You end up talking.

101.title: Lectio divina
101.hook: an old monastic way: read a short passage, notice a word, ponder it, rest
101.howItsDone: Monks and nuns practice lectio divina daily, and many Catholic, Anglican and Protestant Christians use it alone or in small groups, reading a short passage slowly several times, sharing a word that stood out, praying, and resting in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the psalter, the prayer book inside the Bible. Your line was the lord is my shepherd.

How do you read now? Probably fast: scrolling, skimming, headlines, the first two lines of a message and then the next one. In a medieval monastery, a monk sits with a book and reads a single sentence aloud, quietly, to himself. Then again. And again. He isn't trying to finish, or to learn a fact for a test. He's trying to taste it. The monks had a word for this, taken from the way a cow chews the same mouthful over and over, slowly, all afternoon: rumination. And they had a name for the whole practice. It means sacred reading.
screen: `SCROLLING, SKIMMING, LATE.` → `ONE SENTENCE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `CHEWING IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Lectio divina is Latin: divine reading, sacred reading. Saint Benedict, who wrote a rule for monks in the sixth century, set aside hours every day for it. In the twelfth century a monk named Guigo, the head of a Carthusian monastery in the French Alps, described it as a ladder with four rungs. First, lectio, reading: you read a short passage slowly, often aloud, and notice which word or phrase catches you. Second, meditatio, pondering: you turn that word over, chew it, ask what it's saying to you today. Third, oratio, prayer: you answer God, in your own words, about what you've noticed. Fourth, contemplatio, contemplation, the hardest to explain, because it isn't really doing anything. You rest. You stop talking and simply stay, the way you'd sit with someone you love without needing to speak. Guigo put it in a picture: reading puts the food in your mouth, pondering chews it, prayer tastes it, and contemplation is the sweetness itself. The point isn't to cover much. A whole morning might be spent on one line. That's hard when you want to get through it, but lectio divina says the opposite: go slowly enough and one word is enough. For centuries it lived mostly in monasteries. Today Catholics, Anglicans and many Protestants use it, alone or in small groups, where people read a passage aloud three or four times and each shares the one word that stayed with them. It works best with a short passage; a single verse from the Psalms is plenty. Try this one: "Be still, and know that I am God."

segments.voice: Say that verse, be still, and know that I am God, four times: first slowly, noticing which word catches you, maybe still, maybe know; second, turning that one word over. Third, if you pray, answer God about it; if you don't, answer yourself. Fourth, say it one last time, then rest in the quiet without doing anything at all.
Lectio divina. Latin for sacred reading: read, ponder, pray, rest, with a very few words.

102.title: The examen
102.hook: Ignatius taught a nightly look back: where was God today, where did I miss him?
102.howItsDone: Jesuits and many other Catholics pray the examen once or twice daily, often at night, and many Anglicans and Protestants use it too: giving thanks, asking for light, reviewing the day, asking forgiveness, and looking ahead to tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lectio divina: read, ponder, pray, rest. Your line was one word is enough.

It's late. The house is quiet, and the mind starts its night shift, replaying the worst bits of the day. The awkward thing you said. The email you shouldn't have sent. In 1521, in northern Spain, a young Basque soldier named Iñigo, proud, vain, in love with glory, has his leg smashed by a cannonball defending a fortress. For months he lies in bed. He asks for adventure novels; the house has only a life of Christ and a book of saints' stories. Bored, he reads those, and notices something odd about his own daydreams. That noticing will become a prayer practiced around the world.
screen: `REPLAYING THE DAY.` → `A SOLDIER, A CANNONBALL.` → `NOTICING HIS DAYDREAMS.`

segments.voice: When he daydreamed about winning glory and impressing a great lady, it was exciting at the time, but afterward he felt dry and empty. When he daydreamed about living like the saints, the good feeling stayed. He began to believe God was speaking through those after-feelings. The soldier became Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, and he wrote a manual for prayer called the Spiritual Exercises. In it is a short daily practice called the examen, from the Latin for weighing, like the needle on a scale: a look back over the day, in five steps. First, thanks for today's specific gifts. Second, ask for light, to see the day honestly. Third, walk back through the day, hour by hour: where was God in it? Where did I feel alive, close, grateful? And where did I miss him, turn away, feel empty? Fourth, ask forgiveness for what needs it. Fifth, look ahead to tomorrow with hope. Notice where it starts: not with what you did wrong, but with thanks. It isn't the bedtime replay of your worst moments. It's a search for God in the ordinary hours, like the old prayer in the Psalms: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." The Jesuits have long told the story that Ignatius said his companions could skip other prayers on a busy day, but never the examen. Catholics, Anglicans and many Protestants pray it too, usually at night, in about the time it takes to brush your teeth. Its whole question fits in four words: where was he today?
screen: `DRY, OR CONSOLED?` · `EXAMEN: A WEIGHING.` · `THANKS, LIGHT, REVIEW.` · `SORRY, THEN HOPE.` · then, large: `WHERE WAS HE TODAY?`

If you pray, say sorry for what needs it and ask help for tomorrow; if you don't, just note what you've learned.

103.title: Arrow prayers (Nehemiah 2:4)
103.hook: before the king answers, Nehemiah fires a silent prayer upward
103.howItsDone: Many Christians pray short, silent prayers through the day, before a meeting, at a siren, in a moment of fear, alongside longer times of prayer; Orthodox Christians often use the Jesus Prayer this way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the examen: Ignatius's nightly look back over the day. Your line was where was he today? Today, a prayer that takes about one second.

Someone important turns to you and says: so, what do you want? The interview. The doctor. The boss with one minute between meetings. Your mouth is open, and there's no time to think. The same question once came in the Persian court, about four and a half centuries before Jesus. A Jewish man named Nehemiah is cupbearer to King Artaxerxes: he serves the king's wine. He's just heard that the walls of Jerusalem are rubble, and he can't hide his grief. The king notices his sad face, and the text says, "Then I was very sore afraid." A sad servant in front of a king was a risk. Then the king asks the question. What do you want? Nehemiah has maybe a second.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU WANT?` → `A CUPBEARER TO A KING.` → `ONE SECOND TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And in the very next breath, he answers the king. No words recorded, no kneeling, no closed eyes. Between the question and the answer, a prayer went up, and nobody in the room saw it. Christians came to call this an arrow prayer: short, silent, fired upward in the middle of life. Augustine wrote of monks in the Egyptian desert, the same desert as the Jesus Prayer, who prayed all day in quick, brief bursts. But the arrow didn't come from nowhere. In chapter one, when the bad news first came, Nehemiah sat down and wept, and fasted and prayed for days. Months passed before the king ever asked. So the arrow flew from a bow that had been strung for a long time. The long prayer and the short one belong together. The Bible is full of these arrows. A mother pleading for her daughter, in Matthew: "Lord, help me." Peter, sinking into the waves: "Lord, save me." Three words each. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all have their short prayers for the middle of things. For Nehemiah, it worked: the king said yes, and he went home to rebuild the wall.

segments.voice: Think of the next conversation you'll have today, with a coworker, a child, a cashier, someone on the phone, and picture the moment before the first word. If you pray, send up a short line in three seconds, like the mother's "Lord, help me," or a few words of your own; if you don't, take one slow breath and wish them well. Then let the rest of the time be quiet.

104.title: Praying for others by name
104.hook: Christians pray for people by name, trusting God hears
104.howItsDone: Christians pray for others by name in private prayer and in church: the prayers of the people in many liturgies, the reading of names in Orthodox services, and prayer lists and prayer chains in many Protestant churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arrow prayers: Nehemiah's one-second prayer before the king. Your line was short prayers fly.

Somebody texts you: please pray for my dad, surgery Thursday. Maybe you pray; maybe you don't know what to do with that. The request is old, and Exodus has a picture of it. In a battle, Moses stands on a hill above Israel with his arms raised. While his hands are up, the story says, Israel prevails; when they drop, Israel loses ground. Arms get heavy. So his brother Aaron and a man named Hur sit Moses on a stone and hold his arms up, one on each side, until sunset. In the King James, "Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands." Some Christian readers see in that picture prayer for someone else.
screen: `PLEASE PRAY FOR MY DAD.` → `ARMS ON A HILL.` → `AARON AND HUR HOLD THEM UP.`

segments.voice: Intercession comes from Latin, to go between: stepping in for someone, standing between them and what they're facing, and bringing them before God. The New Testament puts it on the list early. Paul writes to Timothy: "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men." First of all, for all people. The Bible is full of people praying for others. Abraham bargains with God over a whole city. Jesus tells Peter, before Peter's worst night, that he has prayed for him, that his faith would not fail. On the cross, Luke says, Jesus prays: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Notice the names. Paul's letters are crowded with them, and he tells his friends he remembers them in his prayers. A name makes it real: not the sick in general, but Marta, in room four. Churches do it differently. In Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran services, the prayers of the people bring the sick, the grieving and the world before God. In Orthodox liturgy, the priest reads out names of the living and the departed. Many evangelical churches run prayer chains, a phone tree praying for whoever needs it this week. Catholics and Orthodox Christians also ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend; many Protestants ask only God, and their friends still on earth. All share James's plain instruction: "pray one for another." Nobody claims to know exactly how it works. Christians say God hears, and that holding someone up changes something, often in the one who holds.

105.title: How long, O Lord? (Psalm 13)
105.hook: the Bible gives you permission to complain to God
105.howItsDone: Christians pray the lament psalms in daily prayer, at funerals and in times of crisis, and many churches hold services of lament after tragedies; some people write their own complaints to God in a journal, following the psalms' shape.

segments.voice: Yesterday, intercession: hold them up. This week, ways to pray: the Jesus Prayer, the Psalms, lectio divina, the examen, arrows, names.

It's two in the morning. The diagnosis hasn't changed. The job hasn't come through. The person hasn't called back. You've been polite about it for months, and an impolite question is building. Many people assume two options: swallow it, or walk away from God entirely. The Bible offers a third, in its own prayer book: a psalm that opens with a complaint and doesn't apologize for it. In the King James words: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" That's somebody at the end of their rope, talking straight to God.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `SWALLOW IT, OR WALK AWAY?` → `A THIRD WAY: HOW LONG?`

segments.voice: Lament: a prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God. You met this psalm on day seventeen, with David shouting at God. Today, the shape is the teaching. The first two verses ask how long, four times. Then a request: "Consider and hear me, O LORD my God: lighten mine eyes." Look at me. Answer me. Then the turn: "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." Complaint, request, trust. And nothing outside has changed. No answer arrives between verse four and verse five. The turn happens in the one praying. Scholars count around a third of the Psalms as laments, and some are a whole people's cry, after a defeat or a famine. Not all of them turn; Psalm 88 never does. Lamentations, a whole book of lament, grieves Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it, and four of its five chapters are acrostics: each verse starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Grief, set out from A to Z. Some readers hear in that a way of saying all of it, every letter, and of giving pain a shape with an end. You don't complain to someone you think isn't there. A lament keeps talking to God while saying, this hurts, and it isn't right. Jews have prayed these psalms for many centuries, and on Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the temple, Lamentations is chanted aloud. Christians of every church pray the laments too. For both, honesty isn't the opposite of faith. Sometimes it's what faith sounds like at two in the morning.
screen: `HOW LONG? FOUR TIMES.` · `COMPLAINT, REQUEST, TRUST.` · `GRIEF FROM A TO Z.` · then, large: `YOU DON'T COMPLAIN TO NOBODY.`

segments.voice: On paper or your phone, write the thing you've been polite about for too long, in one or two plain sentences. If you pray, start the way the psalm does, how long; if you don't, write it to whoever or whatever you'd want to hear it. Don't tidy it up or add a happy ending unless one comes; then sit with it.
Lament. A prayer of grief and complaint, spoken to God rather than about him.
